In Defense of Bubbles

Mania as a coordination device

Some infrastructure only gets built by people who are collectively, temporarily wrong.

2 min read2 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected 2 timesUpdated 20 September 2026
On this pageBy the numbersHow it happenedWho did the workWhere it is contestedCorrectedWhat I changed my mind aboutGo to the sourceReads across to

Britain's railway mania destroyed a generation of investors and left Britain with a railway network. Those are the same sentence.

If you keep one line

Ask what's left standing when the money burns. Buildable assets forgive manias; fixed ones don't.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

At the peak in 1846, Parliament passed 263 Acts authorising some 9,500 miles of new railway; about a third of it was never built and a great deal of the capital was never seen again. What survived was a network. The dot-com bubble did the same trick with fibre: enormous sums went into laying capacity, much of it sat dark after the bust, and the next twenty years of internet traffic ran over infrastructure bought at prices no rational investor would have paid.

The argument, made most fully by Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber, is that bubbles solve a coordination problem. Some investments are large, lumpy and complementary — they only pay if many people build at once — and no individual rational actor will move first. A mania is a mechanism for getting everyone to move at once by making them all wrong in the same direction simultaneously. The capital is destroyed; the asset isn't.

This is not a defence of every bubble, and the distinction that matters is what's left standing. A bubble in an asset that can be built — track, fibre, fabs, datacentres — leaves durable capital and a chastened balance sheet. A bubble in an asset fixed in supply, like urban land, mostly transfers wealth to incumbents and then breaks the banking system that financed it, which is a fair description of 2008.

The historical revision is worth having too. Tulip mania is the canonical bubble, and Anne Goldgar's archival work found the crash's actual economic damage to be small and concentrated among a narrow circle of traders. Most of the ruined-nation detail comes from later moralising pamphlets. The most famous bubble in history is mostly a story about how much we enjoy telling stories about bubbles.

01By the numbers

9,500 miBritish railway authorised by 263 Acts in 1846 alone: Wikipedia, 'Railway Mania'
1637Tulip crash, February 1637 — far smaller in real economic effect than the legend: Anne Goldgar, 'Tulip mania: the classic story of a Dutch financial bubble is mostly wrong', The Conversation, 2018

02How it happened

  1. 1637The tulip market breaks. The economic damage is real, narrow, and nothing like the legend.
  2. 1846Railway mania peaks: 263 Acts, 9,500 miles authorised, roughly a third never built.
  3. 1996–2001Post-Telecom Act fibre buildout; much of the capacity sits dark after the crash.
  4. 2007Goldgar's archival study reconstructs what actually happened in 1637 and to whom.
  5. 2008A bubble in fixed-supply assets demonstrates the other kind of outcome.
  6. 2024Hobart and Huber publish 'Boom' and make the coordination argument explicitly.

03Who did the work

Anne GoldgarWent to the Dutch archives and found the most famous bubble in history was mostly a literary genre.
Charles KindlebergerWrote the taxonomy of manias and panics everyone still argues inside of.
Byrne HobartMakes the strongest modern case that some bubbles are load-bearing rather than pathological.

04Where it is contested

Selection bias again: we count the bubbles that left useful infrastructure and quietly forget the ones that left nothing. 'Productive bubble' is far easier to identify afterwards than from inside. And the distribution matters — the people who bear the losses are rarely the ones who capture the surviving asset.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 4 · Aug 2026 · Railway mania mileage.

An early draft said roughly 6,000 miles of British railway were authorised at the peak. The 1846 figure is about 9,500 miles across 263 Acts.

№ 14 · Sept 2026 · Three figures in the Press.

Movable Type said presses were operating in about 205 European cities by 1500, out of more than a thousand. Neither number is in the paper the entry relies on; Fernand Braudel's count, the one found, is 236 towns, and the entry now gives his. Cost Disease said New York subway construction runs about $1.5 billion a kilometre. The Transit Costs Project's own New York study puts Phase 1 of the Second Avenue Subway at about $1.7 billion a kilometre, and the entry now says so. In Defense of Bubbles said 85 to 95 per cent of the fibre laid in the 1990s sat dark after the bust. Every account found attributes the range to unnamed analysts, and no study behind it could be opened, so the number is gone.

06What I changed my mind about

I used to think the lesson was 'bubbles are underrated'. It's narrower: bubbles in buildable, non-rival assets are underrated, and bubbles in fixed-supply assets are exactly as bad as everyone says. Which type you're in is knowable in advance, and it's the only part of the question that's decidable in advance.

For the Acts-and-mileage figures, which are more dramatic than the summaries suggest.

Water in the West — the 1922 Compact divided more water than the river carries, on flow estimates from unusually wet years. Collective, temporary wrongness, and the concrete is still there.

Edward O. Thorp — the person who had to price the thing in practice, and whose rule says how much to stake once you think the crowd is wrong.
